qs.q: Natural Killer (NK) cells are part of the innate immune system and primarily target:
o: Targeting virally infected cells and tumor cells
qs.e: NK cells are lymphocytes of the innate immune system that recognize and kill virally infected cells and tumor cells, typically by detecting changes in MHC Class I expression on their surface.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Natural Killer (NK) cells are innate lymphocytes that kill virus‑infected and transformed cells without prior sensitisation. They act early, guided by missing‑self and stress signals, and shape adaptive immunity.

sections.p: NK cells develop from common lymphoid progenitors and circulate in blood and tissues. They provide rapid cytotoxicity and cytokine release, bridging innate and adaptive immunity.
b: Do not require antigen presentation via MHC I
Recognise ‘missing‑self’ (loss of HLA‑A/B/C) and stress‑induced ligands
Activated by IL‑12, IL‑15, IL‑18 and type I interferons

sections.p: NK cells are large granular lymphocytes containing perforin, granzyme B and cytokines (IFN‑γ, TNF‑α). Their surface receptors include activating (NKG2D, NKp30) and inhibitory (KIR, NKG2A) molecules.
b: Granules release perforin → membrane pores; granzyme B → apoptosis
Inhibitory KIR bind self‑HLA‑class I, preventing auto‑lysis

sections.p: NK cells are not pathogens; this section describes their activation cycle during infection.
b: Resting NK cells patrol blood and tissues
Cytokine storm (e.g., IFN‑α/β) triggers activation and proliferation

sections.p: NK cells themselves rarely cause disease, but quantitative or functional defects predispose to severe viral infections, certain cancers, and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).
b: NK‑cell deficiency → disseminated CMV, EBV, HSV
Hyper‑active NK cells → cytokine storm in HLH

sections.p: Assess NK‑cell number and function when severe viral disease or unexplained cytopenias occur.

t.b: Is the NK‑cell count low? Low count supports NK‑cell deficiency; normal count suggests functional defect.
Does the patient’s NK cells lyse target cells? Impaired lysis indicates functional deficiency; normal lysis rules it out.
Screen for HLH; markedly elevated values suggest hyper‑active NK‑cell driven cytokine storm.

sections.p: Management targets the underlying trigger and supports NK‑cell function.
b: Antiviral therapy (e.g., ganciclovir for CMV) when infection is identified
Immunoglobulin or interferon‑α to boost NK activity in some viral illnesses
HLH: etoposide‑based regimens plus dexamethasone; avoid cyclosporine if renal failure

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams.
b: NK cells kill without prior sensitisation – missing‑self concept
Low NK count → severe viral infections; high activity → HLH
IL‑12/IL‑15 are essential cytokines for NK activation

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly progressive fever with cytopenias and organ failure (possible HLH)
Severe, refractory viral infection (CMV, EBV) in a child or immunocompromised adult

faq.q: Why do NK cells not need antigen presentation?
faq.a: They recognise stress ligands and loss of self‑MHC, bypassing the need for peptide‑MHC presentation.
Inhibitory KIR receptors detect normal HLA‑I; loss of HLA‑I removes inhibition, triggering NK killing.

faq.q: Can NK‑cell numbers be normal in functional deficiency?
faq.a: Yes; functional assays are required when clinical suspicion remains despite normal counts.

exam: Explain how NK cells distinguish healthy from infected cells and why this is clinically important.
A child presents with disseminated CMV and low NK‑cell activity. Outline the diagnostic work‑up and immediate management.
Describe the pathophysiology of HLH related to NK‑cell hyper‑activity and its key laboratory clues.
